title: Psalm 56: When I Am Afraid, I Trust in You
summary: Hounded by enemies who twist his words and watch his steps, David asks God for mercy and answers his own fear with trust. A refrain asks, “What can man do to me?” The psalm ends with a vow of thanksgiving, as though the rescue he prayed for has already come.
story: Psalm 56 opens a run of five psalms (56 to 60) that each carry the label Miktam, and it stands in the long Davidic collection of Book II (Psalms 51 to 65). Psalms 51 to 59 lean heavily on the stories of David's years as a hunted man in 1 Samuel, and this one is tied to one of the lowest moments of those years: David, anointed but not yet king, fled from Saul into Philistine territory and found himself in danger there too. The psalm moves from fear to trust to thanksgiving, a pattern that the Psalter repeats many times, and it gives words to the experience of being caught between two hostile powers with no human refuge left.
historical:
The heading places the psalm “when the Philistines seized him in Gath.” The best-known account is 1 Samuel 21:10-15, where David fled from Saul to Achish, king of Gath, was recognized by the king's servants as the celebrated warrior of Israel, and escaped only by pretending to be insane. Gath was one of the five chief Philistine cities, on the coastal plain west of Judah, and its site at Tell es-Safi has been extensively excavated. The Samuel narrative doesn't say David was seized, so some readers take the heading as a summary of his danger there, while others think it refers to an episode Samuel doesn't record. Psalm 34 is also linked to this event.

The superscriptions are old, but whether they are original is debated. The Hebrew phrase translated “of David” can mean written by David, belonging to a Davidic collection, or dedicated to him. Many traditional readers take the historical notes as reliable memory of when a psalm was composed. Many critical scholars think later editors added them, matching a psalm's language to a scene from Samuel so that readers could pray it alongside David's story. Both views agree that the heading invites the reader to hear the psalm in David's mouth at that moment. The meaning of Miktam is uncertain; the Greek translation (the Septuagint, made by Jewish scholars in the last centuries before Christ) took it as an inscription. The tune name, “A Dove on Distant Oaks,” is an ancient melody we can no longer identify.
cultural:
Two vivid images come from ordinary life. Verse 8 asks God to “Put my tears in Your bottle,” using the word for a skin bottle, the goatskin or sheepskin bag in which people carried water, wine, and milk. A tear saved in such a container is a tear treasured and remembered, not spilled on the ground and lost. The same verse speaks of God's book, drawing on the familiar picture of a king's records in which deeds and debts were written down (compare Exodus 32:32 and Malachi 3:16). The God who keeps accounts of sin also keeps an account of his servant's sorrow.

The ending reflects Israel's practice of vows. A person in danger often promised to bring a thank offering to the sanctuary if God delivered them, and paying the vow afterward was a public act of worship in which the rescued person told others what God had done (Leviticus 7:11-15 describes the thank offering). When David says “Your vows are upon me,” he means he is under obligation to keep his promise, and he intends to.
literary: The psalm is an individual lament that turns into thanksgiving. It is built around a refrain that appears first in verse 4 and again, expanded, in verses 10 and 11: praise for God's word, trust in God, refusal to fear, and the question “What can man do to me?” In the second version the divine name the LORD is added beside God, one of the few places in this part of the Psalter (where Elohim, God, dominates) that uses both. Each stanza sets the enemies' constant pressure (the Hebrew phrase for all day appears in verses 1, 2, and 5) against the speaker's settled trust. Verse 8 contains a wordplay the English can't show: the word for wanderings (nod) sounds exactly like the word for a skin bottle (nod). God counts the one and stores the other.

outline.t: A plea for mercy against relentless enemies
Refrain: in God I trust, I will not be afraid
Twisted words, plots, and a call for judgment
Tears in God's bottle, wanderings in his book
Refrain expanded: what can man do to me
Vows paid and a life walked in the light

doctrines.note: Trust here is not the absence of fear but its answer: “When I am afraid, I put my trust in You.” Faith is a deliberate turning toward God while the danger is still present, grounded in his word rather than in the speaker's feelings.
God is pictured as keeping account of every wandering step and every tear. Nothing in the sufferer's life is lost or unnoticed, even when rescue has not yet arrived.

The psalm moves from petition to confidence to thanksgiving and vows. Prayer in the Psalms often begins in distress and ends in praise, not because circumstances changed mid-prayer but because the one praying has remembered who God is.

words.note: Batach, to trust, to feel secure in someone. It appears three times in this short psalm (verses 3, 4, and 11). The verb describes resting one's weight on something, and the Psalms constantly ask what a person is leaning on: horses, riches, princes, or God. Here trust is set directly against fear.

Davar, word. The refrain praises God's word, and the enemies twist David's words. The contrast is deliberate: human words are distorted and used as weapons, while God's word is reliable enough to praise. The promise God had given David, perhaps his anointing as future king, is likely in view.

Dimah, tears. The noun appears in several laments (Psalm 6:6; 39:12; 42:3). In verse 8 tears are not a sign that God is absent but something he collects and keeps, which gives grief a dignity and a hearing before God.

Or, light. The psalm ends with walking “before God in the light of life.” Light in the Old Testament is a common picture of life, safety, and God's favor, the opposite of the darkness of death that David has escaped.

christ: The refrain “What can man do to me?” has a close parallel in Psalm 118:6, which the letter to the Hebrews quotes to assure believers that the Lord is their helper (Hebrews 13:6). Paul's question in Romans 8:31, if God is for us, who can be against us, expresses the same confidence as verse 9, where the Hebrew says literally that God is for me. Those are shared themes rather than predictions. Jesus himself had his words twisted by enemies who watched him and plotted against him (Luke 11:53-54; 20:20), and he entrusted himself to the Father rather than to any human protector. The closing line about walking in “the light of life” finds an echo in Jesus' promise that whoever follows him will have the light of life (John 8:12).
questions: David says, “When I am afraid, I put my trust in You.” What would it look like for you to trust God while still feeling afraid, rather than waiting for the fear to go away first?
What difference does it make to believe that God keeps a record of your tears and wanderings?
The psalm ends with a vow to give thanks. How could you mark God's help publicly when a hard season ends?
